overview: Latvia declared independence in 1918. Its interwar republic redistributed farmland and built universities, factories and public markets. Parliamentary democracy ended in the 1934 coup. Occupation in 1940 destroyed practical independence, although the Latvian state continued to exist in international law.

periods.title: Building the republic
periods.summary: A constituent assembly created a constitution and parliamentary institutions.

periods.title: Authoritarian rule
periods.summary: The May 1934 coup ended parliamentary government.

periods.title: Wartime occupations
periods.summary: Soviet, German and renewed Soviet occupation brought repression, persecution and war.

items.text: The 1922 constitution gave voting rights to qualifying Latvian citizens of both sexes over 21. The first Saeima election drew more than 800,000 voters. Voting was a new way to shape the country, although the 1934 coup later closed parliament.

Land reform between 1920 and 1937 broke up large holdings. Land entered a State Land Fund and was redistributed to other residents as private property. For families receiving land, the republic’s decisions changed who controlled the fields and the future of a farm.

The University of Latvia began in 1919 with nine faculties, including medicine, engineering, chemistry, agriculture and architecture. Veterinary medicine joined in 1920. Training people to design buildings, treat patients and care for farm animals belonged to the same effort to build a new state.

In 1920, Riga’s new medical faculty received a former Orthodox seminary building. It became the Anatomikum, later housing anatomy, physiology, hygiene, microbiology and other departments. Students also learned in city hospitals, including the children’s hospital. Medical education needed laboratories and real clinical practice.

Riga’s radio service officially opened on 1 November 1925 with a transmission of Puccini’s opera Madame Butterfly. Experimental broadcasts had begun in October. A performance in the opera house could now reach listeners through a radio receiver, giving live music a new route into people’s homes.

VEF in Riga began industrial production of Walter Zapp’s Minox camera in 1938, following his Tallinn prototype. Tallinn’s Photography Museum preserves an early Riga-made example with serial number 118 and its leather case. Making a tiny camera reliably was a factory achievement as well as an inventor’s idea.

Riga’s Freedom Monument was unveiled on 18 November 1935. Residents’ donations financed Kārlis Zāle’s monument to independence and those who had died fighting for it. Granite and copper turned a public fundraising effort into a lasting landmark.

Riga’s new Central Market opened in 1930 under roof structures reused from German Zeppelin hangars. Engineers used only their upper sections and built lower brick and concrete supports. Keeping the enormous original height would have made indoor temperatures difficult to manage. Even a market roof had to think about the groceries.

The market combined electric lighting and central heating with an extensive basement network. Passages below the pavilions helped move and store goods away from the bustle above. Shopping depended on a less visible working world beneath the stalls.

Ķemeri’s state-funded hotel opened in 1936 with hydrotherapy rooms on its ground floor, allowing the resort to offer treatments throughout the year. Museum postcards show mud being collected and baths being prepared. These were historical treatment practices; the hotel’s architecture and equipment reveal the investment behind them.

Ķemeri also hosted major chess tournaments in 1937 and 1939 to attract visitors. A health resort could sell peaceful surroundings, social life and the excitement of a match. The spectators’ hearts may have raced even when the players remained firmly seated.

Latvian, article 1 of the constitution adopted in 1922: “Latvija ir neatkarīga demokrātiska republika.” Translation: “Latvia is an independent democratic republic.” The sample follows the official 1993 republication of the earlier constitutional text.

ending.text: The USSR occupied and illegally annexed Latvia in 1940. Nazi occupation followed, then Soviet rule returned during the war. Latvia retained legal state continuity and restored full independence in 1991. The map’s 1945 endpoint is not the date independence was first lost.
